prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: Across frames 1–3, the bicycle wheel/handlebar assembly is the nearest major object, about 0.3–0.8 m in front of the camera wearer, with the workbench, monitors, and tools roughly 1–3 m beyond it; the wearer’s visible forearms/hands are also very near, about 0.2–0.6 m away. The bright curved wheel makes its depth and partial occlusion of the bench clearer than in RGB, while darker background regions indicate greater distance. In frames 4–5 the camera turns or moves right and closer to the bicycle, so the frame becomes dominated by nearby bicycle parts and the wearer’s body, with much of the room occluded or outside view. Metric distances are only rough because brightness changes abruptly, thin bicycle structures are incomplete, and several background surfaces receive implausibly similar depths.
descriptions.segmentation: In frames 1–2, a large motorcycle-labelled mask occupies the left/front region where the RGB shows a bicycle and equipment, extending from roughly 0.4 m away toward the work area; this label is unreliable, although the mask helps separate the large foreground structure from the background. Frame 3 contains almost no detected instances despite the bicycle remaining visible, while frame 4 marks a small upper object as an umbrella even though that classification is not supported by the RGB. In frame 5, masks labelled person, person, and car appear on overlapping bicycle/wearer regions near the centre-right, roughly 0.2–1 m from the camera, but these identities and boundaries are clearly unreliable. The map can expose overlap and partial visibility, yet it does not consistently represent the actual bicycle, wearer, bench, monitors, or tools, so it cannot reliably establish interpersonal spacing, facing direction, or gaze.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is completely black in all five frames, so it detects no body or hand skeletons and provides no usable joint, facing, gaze, reach, or person-to-person geometry. From the RGB, parts of the camera wearer’s arms and hands lie at the lower edge and remain within roughly 0.2–0.6 m, near or touching the bicycle assembly, but the map does not recover them. No other person is clearly resolved well enough to infer position, orientation, or distance, and any body-like regions are heavily occluded or partly outside the frame. Its failure across the sequence is itself evidence that pose estimation is unreliable here, likely because the egocentric limbs are cropped and the scene is dominated by overlapping bicycle structures.
